# On the Strange Comfort of Unfinished Things

I've been thinking lately about incompleteness, and how it's become something of a relief in a world obsessed with closure.

There's this painting in my mind—not one I've seen, but one I imagine exists somewhere. It's a landscape, I think, maybe a hillside with a figure standing in the middle distance. The artist abandoned it midway through. The sky is rendered in full, brilliant detail, but the figure is merely sketched in charcoal. One arm is complete; the other trails away into nothing. The grass is suggested rather than stated, a few green strokes that never quite resolve into coherence.

I find this imaginary painting comforting. There's something about it that feels more honest than a finished work ever could be.

We live in an age of completion anxiety. Everything must be tied up, explained, resolved. Television shows end (sometimes controversially). Books conclude. Relationships are officially closed or remain in that purgatory of ambiguity that modern dating has created. Our creative endeavors go through drafts until we can't see them anymore, until we either declare them done or abandon them in frustration. There's rarely permission to simply stop, to say: this is what I have, this is where it led me, and I'm leaving it here.

But I think about the Sagrada Familia in Barcelona, that towering cathedral that's been under construction for over a century. I think about how many people have walked through its doors knowing it will outlive them, knowing they're experiencing something perpetually becoming. There's a peculiar magic in that. You can't take a cathedral's completion for granted. You can't say you've seen it. You can only say you've seen it in this particular moment of its endless becoming.

I used to write stories obsessively. Short fiction mostly, because short fiction felt achievable. I could finish a story in an afternoon, a few hours even. The satisfaction of typing "THE END" was like a small hit of something necessary. I filled folders with these completed things. And yet, I barely remember any of them. What I do remember, vividly, are the stories I never finished. There's one about a woman who discovers her neighbor is living the life she would have lived. I wrote about thirty pages. The premise is a question, a knot, an itch that won't be scratched. I've thought about this story more in the years since abandoning it than I did in the months I was writing it.

Maybe there's something about incompleteness that forces the reader—or the thinker—to become a co-creator. A finished work is received. It's done to you. But an unfinished work requires something from you. It asks you to complete it in the privacy of your own mind. It trusts you with its gaps.

I think about conversations I've had that trailed off naturally, without resolution. Someone says something that needs sitting with, and we both recognize it. We go quiet. The conversation has reached its natural ending point, which isn't an ending at all, just a place where the talking stops but the thinking doesn't. These feel more valuable to me than conversations that tie themselves up neatly with conclusions and exchanged phone numbers.

There's a Japanese aesthetic called *ma*—the concept of negative space, emptiness, the space between things. It's not merely absence; it's presence through absence. A room with too much furniture in it can feel cramped, but a sparsely furnished room with the right proportions feels spacious and generous. The empty space isn't a failure of decoration; it's the whole point. Similarly, an unfinished work isn't a work with something missing; it's a work that acknowledges its own limits and trusts the space beyond those limits to matter.

I've been rereading Montaigne's essays, which are gloriously incomplete. They circle around ideas rather than arriving at them. He contradicts himself without apparent distress. His essays end when they end, not because he's solved the problem but because he's reached some kind of working truce with it. The form itself—the essay, from the French *essai*, meaning attempt—is built on this principle. You're not writing a treatise. You're making an attempt. The attempt itself is the point.

There's something deeply humbling about acknowledging that you can't complete something. That the project is bigger than you, more complex than you anticipated, more interesting precisely because it resists your attempts at mastery over it. A lot of perfectionism is really about control—the need to shape something completely, to leave no loose threads, to make it impossible for anyone else to misunderstand or misinterpret. But life itself is loose threads and misunderstandings. Life is fundamentally incomplete, and perhaps our work should acknowledge that rather than pretend to transcend it.

I think about the people I've loved and lost touch with. The friendships that fizzled rather than ended. Are these failures? Sometimes I used to think so. But increasingly I see them as complete in their incompleteness. We knew each other for as long as we knew each other. The friendship wasn't a project with a disappointing conclusion; it was a period, and periods end, and that's not tragic—that's just rhythm.

Maybe the goal isn't to finish things but to engage with them as fully as possible before moving on. Maybe the artistic endeavor isn't to achieve some perfect, unchangeable form but to mark a moment when you had to stop, when the work had taught you what it needed to teach you, when you had to trust that it would survive without you.

There's a freedom in that. There's permission in that.

So I'm learning to be okay with the unfinished painting, the story that stops mid-gesture, the conversation that trails away, the life that doesn't resolve into the narrative I expected. I'm learning that incompleteness might not be a failure but a different kind of completion altogether—the completion of accepting that some things will always be becoming, and that might be their greatest strength.

The sky remains brilliant. The figure remains suggested. The grass remains a sketch. And somehow, in that refusal to finish, the work is finally whole.
